patient.title: Trifluridine/tipiracil (Lonsurf) monotherapy

agents.name: Trifluridine/tipiracil
agents.mechanism: Damages cancer-cell DNA while slowing breakdown of the active drug
agents.explanation: Trifluridine is incorporated into DNA and interferes with cell growth. Tipiracil slows its breakdown so more trifluridine can reach the bloodstream. Healthy cells can also be affected; blood counts and symptoms need monitoring.
agents.watch: Check the exact dosing and rest days. Report fever, sudden illness, vomiting, diarrhoea, bleeding or reduced urine promptly.
risks: Low blood counts: infection, anaemia and bleeding
Fatigue, reduced appetite and mouth soreness
Kidney impairment can increase treatment toxicity
Pregnancy harm and important contraception requirements

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: What if I miss a dose or vomit?
questions.a: Do not make up a missed, held or vomited dose and do not double the next dose. Tell your team and follow the next scheduled dose on the agreed calendar. Repeated vomiting needs advice because of dehydration and missed medicines.

questions.q: Are tablet-free days safe days?
questions.a: No. The rest period allows recovery, but low blood counts and other problems can occur then too. Use the same urgent contact plan throughout the cycle.

questions.q: Can my morning and evening tablet numbers differ?
questions.a: Yes. The pharmacy may prescribe different morning and evening quantities to match the correct total daily dose. Do not assume the same number or substitute tablet strengths; follow the written label and calendar.

questions.q: Is the bevacizumab combination evidence the same?
questions.a: No. A study of Lonsurf plus bevacizumab tests an additional medicine and its extra risks. Its results should not be presented as the expected benefit of Lonsurf on its own.

patient.urgent_extra: Call your oncology team immediately for a temperature of 37.5°C or above, 36°C or below, shivering or suddenly feeling unwell. Infection can occur without a fever. Call urgently for bleeding, severe diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, inability to drink, very little urine or new breathlessness. Severe breathing difficulty, heavy bleeding or collapse needs 112 / 999.

items.title: Take tablets after meals
items.text: Swallow the prescribed tablets with water within one hour after finishing breakfast and the evening meal on dosing days. items.title: Two blocks of five days
items.text: Take the prescribed morning and evening tablets on Days 1–5, have no Lonsurf on Days 6–7, then take morning and evening tablets on Days 8–12. Days 13–28 are tablet-free. A new 28-day cycle starts only when the team authorises it.

items.title: Baseline and each cycle
items.text: Blood count, kidney and liver tests and urine-protein screening are required. Additional blood counts may be needed during treatment, especially with kidney impairment.

items.title: Why a new cycle may wait
items.text: The blood-count requirements for starting another cycle are different from the thresholds for stopping tablets during a cycle. Symptoms, prior severe low counts, time to recover and the current prescription all matter.

items.title: Dose changes
items.text: Your team may delay treatment or use a lower dose after toxicity. Do not restart from a diary or increase the dose after a reduction. Tablet quantities are checked by pharmacy.

items.text: This oral medicine has moderate-to-high sickness risk. Agree a preventive and rescue anti-sickness plan with the team. If you cannot keep fluids or medicines down, call; do not add or repeat doses yourself.

items.title: Food, fluids and bowel symptoms
items.text: Take tablets after meals as instructed. Drink as your team advises and report diarrhoea, repeated vomiting, poor intake or reduced urine early. A prescribed bowel treatment plan does not replace urgent assessment.

items.title: Contraception and fertility
items.text: Discuss fertility before treatment. Women need highly effective contraception during treatment and for six months after; add a barrier method to hormonal contraception. Men with a partner who could become pregnant need effective contraception during treatment and for six months afterwards. Do not breastfeed while taking this medicine.

items.title: Other medicines
items.text: Tell the pharmacist about all prescribed, non-prescription and herbal medicines, including antivirals. Keep tablets safely in their supplied packaging and follow disposal advice.

evidence.title: Evidence for colorectal monotherapy
evidence.intro: RECOURSE compared Lonsurf plus supportive care with placebo plus supportive care in previously treated metastatic colorectal cancer.
evidence.population: Adults with refractory metastatic colorectal cancer and ECOG 0–1.
evidence.interpretation: The trial found longer survival with Lonsurf than placebo in this selected population. A group result cannot predict an individual benefit. Gastric treatment and Lonsurf with bevacizumab are different evidence contexts.
evidence.limitations: SUNLIGHT studied adding bevacizumab and TAGS studied gastric cancer. Neither is the benefit estimate for this colorectal monotherapy pathway.

patient.title: Atezolizumab + bevacizumab for HCC

agents.name: Atezolizumab
agents.alias: Tecentriq; IV infusion or thigh injection
agents.mechanism: Helps immune cells recognise and attack cancer
agents.explanation: Blocking PD-L1 can release a brake on the immune response. This may control cancer but can also cause inflammation in healthy organs during treatment or after it stops.
visual: Cancer and healthy tissues may be affected
agents.watch: Carry the immunotherapy alert card. Report new bowel, breathing, skin, hormone, heart, liver, kidney or neurological symptoms promptly.
risks: Immune inflammation of lungs, bowel, liver, kidneys or skin
Hormone changes, including thyroid, adrenal or pituitary problems and diabetes; replacement may be long term
Rare serious heart, muscle, nerve or brain inflammation
Infusion/injection reactions; delayed immune effects after stopping

agents.name: Bevacizumab
agents.alias: Avastin or prescribed biosimilar; IV infusion
agents.mechanism: Blocks a signal for blood-vessel growth
agents.explanation: Bevacizumab binds VEGF, reducing signals that help tumours develop blood vessels. It can also affect normal blood vessels, blood pressure, kidney filtration and wound healing.
visual: Blood vessels and healing need monitoring
agents.watch: Report bleeding, severe headache, chest or abdominal pain, leg swelling, reduced urine or poor wound healing. Tell the team before surgery or dental procedures.
risks: Raised blood pressure; rarely hypertensive crisis or PRES
Protein in urine and kidney injury, including nephrotic syndrome
Bleeding, including serious bleeding from varices
Poor wound healing, bowel perforation or fistula; rare jaw problems

questions.q: Does having more side effects mean treatment is working?
questions.a: No. Side effects do not reliably show whether the cancer is responding. Report them so they can be treated. Your team assesses benefit using the tests and review plan appropriate to your cancer.

questions.q: Why might a dose be delayed or reduced?
questions.a: Your team may allow recovery, investigate a symptom or reduce the chance of lasting harm. Ask which drug changes, why, and when review is planned. A delay does not itself mean treatment has failed.

questions.q: What should I say when calling?
questions.a: Give the regimen name, last treatment date, symptoms and when they started. Explain whether you can eat, drink, pass urine and manage usual activities. Give your temperature if available, but do not delay calling to collect details.

questions.q: What belongs in the consent conversation?
questions.a: The individual aim and likely benefit, uncertainty, reasonable alternatives including not proceeding, common and serious risks, lasting effects, fertility and practical concerns. You can ask for an interpreter, more time or another explanation and can reconsider your decision.

questions.q: How many cycles should I use this passport for?
questions.a: The passport provides reusable recording pages, not a prescribed course length. Your oncology team sets the duration and can provide extra pages.

questions.q: Can I use this page to decide if blood results are safe?
questions.a: No. Treatment decisions require the clinical protocol, symptoms, previous toxicity, organ function and the prescriber’s review. The patient page explains the checks and does not authorise treatment.

questions.q: Why do I need a check for varices?
questions.a: Liver disease can cause enlarged veins in the food pipe or stomach that may bleed. Bevacizumab can increase bleeding risk. The team checks for varices and treats any relevant risk before starting; having the test alone does not mean the risk has been controlled.

questions.q: Does an abnormal liver test always mean immune hepatitis?
questions.a: No. Liver cancer, underlying liver disease, infection, blocked bile flow and medicines can all affect results. The team compares results with your baseline and investigates the cause before deciding how each medicine changes.

questions.q: Can one medicine be held while the other continues?
questions.a: Sometimes. The reason for holding treatment, your general condition and the source rules for each medicine determine the plan. Never assume that stopping one means the other is automatically safe to continue.

questions.q: Do immune side effects stop when treatment stops?
questions.a: No. They can begin or persist afterwards. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms, including to doctors outside oncology.

questions.q: Does the thigh injection replace every drip?
questions.a: No. Atezolizumab may be given into the thigh, but bevacizumab remains an infusion into a vein. The two atezolizumab formulations have different doses and must be prescribed correctly.

patient.urgent_extra: Call your oncology team immediately for new breathlessness, persistent diarrhoea, blood or black stools, yellow eyes, dark urine, severe tiredness or dizziness, thirst and frequent urination, unusual weakness, reduced urine or a spreading rash. Tell every healthcare professional that you receive immunotherapy, even after it stops. Vomiting blood, heavy bleeding, sudden severe abdominal or chest pain, stroke symptoms, seizure, collapse or major breathing difficulty need 112 / 999.

chapters.title: Understanding the combination
chapters.intro: Confirm the treatment aim and source eligibility.

items.title: Treatment aim
items.text: This combination aims to control hepatocellular carcinoma, a cancer that starts in the liver, when it is advanced or cannot be removed and no previous systemic treatment has been given. Atezolizumab helps immune cells recognise cancer; bevacizumab blocks a signal that supports blood-vessel growth.

items.title: Liver health matters
items.text: The team checks liver function, cirrhosis, viral-hepatitis management and any ascites or confusion. The pivotal study mainly supports patients with Child-Pugh A liver function; poorer liver function needs specialist discussion.

items.title: Two medicine decisions
items.text: There is no fixed total number of cycles. Clinical benefit, liver function, bleeding risk, immune effects and your preferences guide treatment. One medicine may be paused or stopped while the other is considered separately by the team.

chapters.title: Preparing for the first treatment
chapters.intro: Bleeding-risk review is a separate safety step.

items.title: Varices
items.text: Screening and any required variceal treatment must be reviewed before starting. Call urgently for black stools or blood; vomiting blood or heavy bleeding needs emergency help.

items.title: Baseline checks
items.text: Blood count, kidneys, liver, glucose, thyroid function, urine protein, blood pressure and cardiac history are reviewed. Other tests depend on symptoms, earlier treatment and medicines.

items.title: Consent and route
items.text: Discuss expected benefit and uncertainty, alternatives including not proceeding, liver disease and variceal bleeding, immune toxicity that may be delayed or need lifelong hormone replacement, vascular/kidney/bowel/healing risks, fertility and pregnancy prevention, IV versus thigh administration and your right to reconsider.

chapters.title: Your treatment visit
chapters.intro: The medicines follow a defined sequence.

items.title: IV or thigh atezolizumab
items.text: IV atezolizumab is usually infused over 60 minutes initially and may take 30 minutes later if tolerated. The alternative 1875 mg thigh injection takes about seven minutes. Bevacizumab is still an IV infusion: usually 90 minutes first, then 60 and later 30 minutes if tolerated. Checks, preparation and observation make the whole visit longer.

items.title: During administration
items.text: Tell the nurse immediately about rash, swelling, breathlessness, chest tightness, dizziness or pain at the injection or infusion site. Do not wait until the visit ends.

items.title: Before every cycle
items.text: Blood count, kidney/liver profile, glucose and urine protein are checked before every cycle. Blood pressure is checked before each cycle and after treatment. Thyroid tests are scheduled every six weeks.

chapters.title: Care between visits
chapters.intro: Symptoms can need review between blood tests.

items.title: Blood pressure and urine
items.text: Blood pressure and urine-protein checks are part of each cycle. Continue prescribed blood-pressure medicines and ask before changing them. A positive urine dipstick may need a timed urine collection.

items.title: Immune alert card
items.text: Carry the supplied immunotherapy alert card during treatment and afterwards. New symptoms can need urgent treatment; do not wait for routine blood tests.

items.title: Support medicines
items.text: Both medicines have minimal sickness risk and routine preventive anti-sickness medicines or premedication are not usually required. The team individualises symptom treatment; do not self-treat new significant diarrhoea without advice.

items.title: Surgery, dental work and healing
items.text: Tell oncology before planned procedures and tell your dentist about bevacizumab. Wounds must heal and the team must agree an interruption/restart plan.

chapters.title: Follow-up after treatment
chapters.intro: Continue the contact and alert-card plan.

items.title: Delayed immune effects
items.text: No. They can begin or persist afterwards. Keep the immunotherapy alert card and report new symptoms, including to doctors outside oncology.

items.title: Continuing support
items.text: The team follows ongoing liver, kidney, blood-pressure and hormonal problems and agrees medicine stop dates and next cancer reviews.

items.title: Pregnancy prevention
items.text: Discuss fertility and pregnancy prevention. Atezolizumab requires effective contraception for five months after the last dose and bevacizumab for six months; use the longer interval when both apply. Do not breastfeed during treatment or for at least six months after bevacizumab.

patient.purpose: This combination aims to control hepatocellular carcinoma, a cancer that starts in the liver, when it is advanced or cannot be removed and no previous systemic treatment has been given. Atezolizumab helps immune cells recognise cancer; bevacizumab blocks a signal that supports blood-vessel growth.

evidence.title: Evidence in previously untreated unresectable HCC
evidence.intro: IMbrave150 compared atezolizumab plus bevacizumab with sorafenib in selected people with HCC and preserved liver function.
evidence.population: Previously untreated unresectable HCC, predominantly Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1.
evidence.interpretation: The combination improved survival and time before cancer progressed in the study population. This does not predict an individual outcome or establish the same benefit for more severe liver dysfunction.
evidence.limitations: The trial used IV atezolizumab and excluded important bleeding-risk groups. SC administration is supported by product and NCCP formulation evidence, not a separate HCC survival comparison. Other modern regimens require their own evidence discussion.

anatomy: Tiredness, thirst, dizziness or a new headache may need hormone or neurological review.
New cough or breathlessness needs prompt assessment for lung inflammation and other causes.
Chest pain, palpitations or breathlessness may reflect heart or surrounding-tissue inflammation.
Yellow eyes, dark urine or blood-test changes need cause assessment; liver disease is not automatically immune hepatitis.
Reduced urine or swelling needs review; immune kidney inflammation and bevacizumab protein loss require different assessment.
Diarrhoea, blood or pain can indicate immune colitis; sudden severe pain can signal bowel perforation and needs emergency assessment.
Rash, blisters, weakness, numbness or muscle pain can be immune effects.
Painful swollen joints may need assessment for inflammatory arthritis.
Bleeding, clots, raised blood pressure or delayed wound healing need prompt review.
patient.scope_note: This is the HCC combination, not atezolizumab alone or a lung-cancer chemotherapy combination. Existing liver disease and bleeding risk need review alongside possible immune side effects. Your team assesses each medicine separately.

patient.indication_text: NCCP 00831a: adults with advanced or unresectable HCC without previous systemic therapy; usual source eligibility includes ECOG 0–1 and Child-Pugh A liver function.
patient.anatomy_note: Accepted HCC organ positions are preserved. The medicines can cause overlapping symptoms; the team establishes the cause.
patient.monitoring_summary: FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose, TFTs, oesophageal-varices screening, dipstick protein and BP/cardiac assessment. Consider ECHO after chest-wall radiation or anthracycline; INR if indicated. FBC, renal/liver profile, glucose and dipstick protein before every cycle. Blood pressure before each cycle and after treatment; review clinical toxicity and component-specific decisions. TFTs every six weeks; other tests and imaging according to clinical need and Consultant plan.

clinical.component_rationale: Atezolizumab inhibits PD-L1-mediated immune suppression; bevacizumab inhibits VEGF signalling. The combination has distinct immune, vascular and underlying liver-disease safety domains.
key_points: NCCP 00831a: first systemic therapy for advanced/unresectable HCC; ECOG 0–1, Child-Pugh A.
Atezolizumab 1200 mg IV or 1875 mg SC then bevacizumab 15 mg/kg IV every 21 days; no dose reductions recommended.
Screen and manage oesophageal varices before treatment; recent bleeding/high-risk untreated varices require review.
HCC hepatitis thresholds depend on the matching baseline transaminase category; current LFTs alone do not establish immune causation.
NCCP Table 3 grading is CTCAE v4.0, not v5.0.
Bevacizumab 2+/3+ dipstick requires timed-protein follow-up; >2 to 4 g/24 h holds, >4 discontinues under NCCP. Nephrotic syndrome has an independent SmPC permanent-stop rule.
Persistent grade-3 hypertension, grade-4 VTE, grade≥3 bleeding, perforation and specified fistulae have distinct actions.
Counts are monitored without importing chemotherapy ANC/platelet dose thresholds.

patient_selection.treatment_intent: Disease control in previously untreated advanced/unresectable HCC.
disease_and_biomarker_context: NCCP 00831a: adults with advanced or unresectable HCC without previous systemic therapy; usual source eligibility includes ECOG 0–1 and Child-Pugh A liver function.
No PD-L1 testing requirement is specified for this HCC indication.
eligibility_orientation: Confirm Child-Pugh A, ECOG 0–1, no previous systemic HCC therapy and adequate organ function.
Assess varices, viral hepatitis, ascites, autoimmune disease, immunosuppression, bleeding/clotting and surgery risks.
important_cautions: No equivalent efficacy inference for Child-Pugh B/C or untreated high-risk varices.
Laboratory abnormalities require cause assessment; immune attribution is clinical.
The bevacizumab SmPC does not itself list HCC; HCC combination indication is supported by Tecentriq SmPC and NCCP.

administration: IV atezolizumab is usually infused over 60 minutes initially and may take 30 minutes later if tolerated. The alternative 1875 mg thigh injection takes about seven minutes. Bevacizumab is still an IV infusion: usually 90 minutes first, then 60 and later 30 minutes if tolerated. Checks, preparation and observation make the whole visit longer.
Atezolizumab first, bevacizumab second. SC injection sites alternate thighs; avoid red/bruised/tender/hard skin. Maintain the planned three-week interval when rescheduling missed atezolizumab.
access: Anaphylaxis treatment facilities and suitable IV access are required even when atezolizumab is SC.
Rapid bevacizumab infusion is a separate off-label/local-policy option; it is not the default schedule here.

rationale.summary: This combination aims to control hepatocellular carcinoma, a cancer that starts in the liver, when it is advanced or cannot be removed and no previous systemic treatment has been given. Atezolizumab helps immune cells recognise cancer; bevacizumab blocks a signal that supports blood-vessel growth.
rationale.setting: First-line advanced or unresectable liver cancer (HCC)
factors: Liver function and variceal bleeding risk
Autoimmune/vascular disease, performance status and patient priorities
IV versus SC availability and separate component tolerability
alternatives: Discuss current MDT options, trials and supportive care including not proceeding; avoid cross-trial superiority claims.
limitations: The trial used IV atezolizumab and excluded important bleeding-risk groups. SC administration is supported by product and NCCP formulation evidence, not a separate HCC survival comparison. Other modern regimens require their own evidence discussion.
NCCP source reconciliation and software tests are not independent clinical approval.

evidence.population: 501 patients with previously untreated unresectable HCC, Child-Pugh A and ECOG 0–1, randomised 336 versus 165.
evidence.comparison: Atezolizumab 1200 mg IV plus bevacizumab 15 mg/kg every three weeks versus sorafenib.
evidence.applicability: The combination improved survival and time before cancer progressed in the study population. This does not predict an individual outcome or establish the same benefit for more severe liver dysfunction.

endpoints.metric: Median overall survival from randomisation; 31 August 2020 data cutoff
endpoints.interpretation: Updated ITT analysis; median follow-up 15.6 months. Group estimate for the selected first-line HCC population, not an individual prognosis.
endpoints.analysis_status: Updated published phase III analysis; descriptive p value

endpoints.metric: Median progression-free survival from randomisation; same 31 August 2020 cutoff
endpoints.interpretation: Updated whole-trial PFS; do not combine this endpoint with the earlier primary-analysis time point.

limitations: The trial used IV atezolizumab and excluded important bleeding-risk groups. SC administration is supported by product and NCCP formulation evidence, not a separate HCC survival comparison. Other modern regimens require their own evidence discussion.
Variceal bleeding within six months and untreated/incompletely treated varices with bleeding or high bleeding risk were excluded; safety cannot be assumed from screening alone.
Preserved liver function and trial selection limit extrapolation to decompensated cirrhosis.
evidence.harms: In the updated safety population, treatment-related grade 3–4 events occurred in 43% (143/329) with the combination and 46% (72/156) with sorafenib; treatment-related grade-5 events were 2% (6/329) and <1% (1/156). Types of harm differ; similar aggregate percentages do not make the treatments interchangeable.

milestones.title: Varices review before bevacizumab
milestones.why: Liver disease and anti-VEGF therapy can combine to increase bleeding risk.
milestones.clinical: Screen and treat relevant varices; review recent bleeding.
milestones.action: Confirm the screening result and management plan.

milestones.title: Review each medicine
milestones.why: Immune and anti-VEGF toxicities have different actions.
milestones.clinical: Review blood/urine results, BP, symptoms and liver health.
milestones.action: Record which medicine is held, continued or stopped.

milestones.title: Six-week thyroid monitoring
milestones.why: Thyroid dysfunction can develop without obvious early symptoms.
milestones.clinical: TFTs every six weeks, plus clinical review.
milestones.action: Confirm who books and reviews results.

milestones.title: After treatment
milestones.why: Immune effects may be delayed and other risks persist.
milestones.clinical: Continue alert-card use and follow unresolved effects.
milestones.action: Agree contact, contraception and medicine follow-up.

clinical_notes: This is the HCC combination, not atezolizumab alone or a lung-cancer chemotherapy combination. Existing liver disease and bleeding risk need review alongside possible immune side effects. Your team assesses each medicine separately.

There is no fixed total number of cycles. Clinical benefit, liver function, bleeding risk, immune effects and your preferences guide treatment. One medicine may be paused or stopped while the other is considered separately by the team.
